## What happened

Your push was a non-fast-forward push, so Git rejected it. A non-fast-forward push is a push that does not build on the current remote tip.

The remote branch `main` holds one or more commits that your local `main` does not hold. Another person pushed those commits after your last fetch. Your local `main` and the remote `main` now share a common ancestor, and then split.

Git refuses this push on purpose. A push in this state overwrites the other commits on the remote.

## What to do

1. Run `git fetch origin`. This downloads the remote commits. It does not change your working tree.
2. Run `git log --oneline HEAD..origin/main` to see the commits that you do not hold.
3. Run `git log --oneline origin/main..HEAD` to see your own unpushed commits.
4. Join the two histories. Use `git pull --rebase origin main` for a linear history. Use `git merge origin/main` if your team prefers merge commits.
5. Fix any conflict that the rebase or the merge reports. Then continue with `git rebase --continue`, or commit the merge.
6. Run `git push` again.

## Two cautions

Do not use `git push --force`. That command deletes the other person's commits from the remote.

The rebase in step 4 rewrites your local commits. This is safe here, because you did not push those commits yet. Choose `git merge` instead if you already pushed your commits to another branch, and another person built work on them.
